lesson.title: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge: How a Device Gets an Address
lesson.summary: DHCP automatically assigns a device an IP address, subnet mask, and other network configuration through a four step exchange known as DORA, so that a device joining a network does not need to be configured by hand.
lesson.body:
Every device on an IP network needs an IP address before it can send or receive anything, along with a subnet mask telling it which addresses count as being on its local network versus needing to be routed elsewhere, and usually a default gateway and DNS server addresses as well. Configuring all of that by hand on every laptop, phone, and printer that joins a network would be impractical, which is exactly the problem DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, solves: it lets a device request this configuration automatically the moment it joins a network, and receive it from a DHCP server without any manual setup.

The exchange that accomplishes this is commonly remembered by the acronym DORA, for Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge, and it is worth tracing through carefully because each step exists for a specific reason. A device that has just joined a network, and therefore has no IP address yet and does not know the address of any DHCP server, broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER message to the entire local network, since broadcasting is the only option available to a device that does not yet have an address of its own to send a targeted message from. Any DHCP server on that network segment that receives the discover message can respond with a DHCPOFFER, proposing a specific IP address for the device to use along with a subnet mask, a lease duration, and other configuration such as a default gateway and DNS servers; if more than one DHCP server exists on the network, more than one offer can come back. The device picks one offer and broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST, explicitly stating which offer it is accepting; this is broadcast rather than sent directly to the chosen server so that any other DHCP servers that made offers also see the message and know their offered addresses were not chosen and can be released back into their available pool. Finally, the server whose offer was accepted responds with a DHCPACK, confirming the lease, at which point the device configures its network interface with the assigned address and can begin using the network normally.

A concrete example makes the sequence easier to hold onto. A laptop joins a coffee shop's Wi-Fi network and broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER. The shop's router, acting as the DHCP server, replies with a DHCPOFFER of the address 192.168.1.47, a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0, a default gateway of 192.168.1.1, and a lease time of 24 hours. The laptop broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST confirming it wants 192.168.1.47. The router sends back a DHCPACK, and the laptop finishes configuring itself with that address, that gateway, and that subnet mask, all without anyone typing in a single setting by hand.

This connects directly to two earlier ideas. The subnet mask handed out in the offer is what lets the device figure out, for any address it later wants to reach, whether that address is on its own local network or needs to be sent through the default gateway instead, which only makes sense once a device actually understands what a subnet mask does. And the address 192.168.1.47 in that example is a private address, the kind reserved for use inside local networks; the router assigning it via DHCP is almost always the same device performing NAT, translating traffic from all of these privately addressed devices on the local network out to a single public IP address when it reaches the internet, so DHCP and NAT typically work together on the same router even though they solve two different problems. Leases are not permanent either: a device does not wait until its lease fully expires to renew it, but instead attempts to renew, by sending a new DHCPREQUEST directly to the server it got the lease from, partway through the lease period, so that under normal conditions a device simply keeps its address seamlessly rather than losing connectivity and having to redo the whole DORA process.
